topic: Fractal Dimension: Measuring the Complexity of Shapes

sections.title: The Intuitive Limitation of Euclidean Dimensions
lecture_lines: Traditional dimensions include points, lines, and planes.
Some shapes defy these simple integer measurements.
How complex is a shape filling more space?

sections.title: The Concept of Self-Similarity and Scaling
lecture_lines: Scaling a line by one-third creates three copies.
Scaling a square by one-third creates nine copies.
Dimensions relate number of copies to scaling factor.
animations: Display a unit square, divide it into 3x3 grid [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/grid.svg] (#00FFFF).
Highlight the 9 smaller squares resulting from 1/3 scaling (#FF00FF).
Show formula: N = (1/s)^D floating above the square (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Defining Fractal Dimension (Hausdorff Dimension)
lecture_lines: Fractal dimension quantifies the space-filling capacity.
Calculated as the log of copies over log scale.
The Koch snowflake has a dimension of 1.26.
Non-integer values represent roughness or complexity.
Fractal dimension captures detail at every scale.
animations: Show a line segment being transformed into 4 segments of 1/3 size, replacing the segments with [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/snowflake.svg] shapes to illustrate the recursive construction.
Label result: D ≈ 1.26 prominently below the equation (#FFCC00).

sections.title: Visualizing Complexity in Nature and Technology
lecture_lines: Fractals appear frequently throughout the natural world.
Bronchial trees maximize surface area for gas exchange.
High fractal dimension indicates complex, dense structures.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Fractal dimension measures geometric roughness and complexity.
Lightning bolts possess fractional dimensions between one and two.
This tool quantifies shapes beyond Euclidean limitations.
